Ordinance 2023-184-E approved a redevelopment agreement between the City and the Museum of Science and History of Jacksonville (MOSH) to facilitate the construction of a new “iconic” and integrated museum to be located on City owned property within the Shipyards area

MOSH Contributions Included:
• Construction of new “iconic” museum, requiring:
   - Minimum capital investment of $85,000,000
   - Minimum enclosed space of 75,000 square feet
   - Minimum exhibit space of 50,000 square feet
• Maintenance of 1.5 acres joint-use park (excluding capital maintenance)
• Design surrounding park (reimbursable up to $880,000 by City)

m-jacksonville|2024-06-18|1dcce2a4|e68bb.title: Mr. Peterson explained the amendment which was approved unanimously via a voice vote. Council Member Arias asked if the $6.2M for tree planting is paying for the same kind of trees that were removed and if palm trees are being planted. Curtis Hart, Chair of the Tree Commission, said there is no direct connection between the type of trees being removed and the type being planted. He described the City’s 3 tree-planting project categories. He said the fund has a maximum percentage allowed to be used for palm trees and the Commission tries to plant “the right tree in the right place”. Oak trees must be replaced with oak trees on an inch-for-inch basis. Council Member Lahnen said “exceptional planting projects” have only happened three times in the past three years, so the Council will not be looking at a substantial increase in ordinances processed as a result of this change. Council Member Pittman described a particular constituent’s problem with removal of a protected tree on private property in her district and asked how the average citizen would know that a particular tree is protected. Mr. Hart said he would think about how to possibly designate protected trees on a plat so that owners of at least newly developed properties could be informed. Council Member Pittman said there is a need to inform citizens about protected trees on their property so they know what they can and can’t do with their trees.
